claim: Cardiomyocytes seeding the trabecular layer actively change their shape during cardiac development in zebrafish.
source: Using single cell resolution imaging in zebrafish, we find that cardiomyocytes seeding the trabecular layer actively change their shape while compact layer cardiomyocytes remain static.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental imaging data presented in the manuscript, specifically shown in Figure 1 with time-course 3D imaging of chimeric hearts.

claim: Compact layer cardiomyocytes remain static during trabeculation.
source: Using single cell resolution imaging in zebrafish, we find that cardiomyocytes seeding the trabecular layer actively change their shape while compact layer cardiomyocytes remain static.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental imaging data showing that compact layer CMs do not exhibit morphological changes, as shown in Figure 1d-e".

claim: Erbb2 signaling is required for trabeculation.
source: We show that Erbb2 signaling, which is required for trabeculation, activates glycolysis to support changes in cardiomyocyte shape and behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work and experimental data showing that Erbb2 inhibition impairs trabeculation.

claim: Erbb2 signaling activates glycolysis to support changes in cardiomyocyte shape and behavior.
source: We show that Erbb2 signaling, which is required for trabeculation, activates glycolysis to support changes in cardiomyocyte shape and behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that Erbb2 overexpression upregulates glycolytic enzymes and increases glycolytic activity (Figure 2).

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of glycolysis impairs cardiac trabeculation.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of glycolysis impairs cardiac trabeculation, and cardiomyocyte-specific loss- and gain-of-function manipulations of glycolysis decrease and increase trabeculation, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that DCA treatment reduces the number of CMs in the trabecular layer (Figure 3a).

claim: Cardiomyocyte-specific loss-of-function manipulations of glycolysis decrease trabeculation.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of glycolysis impairs cardiac trabeculation, and cardiomyocyte-specific loss- and gain-of-function manipulations of glycolysis decrease and increase trabeculation, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that pdha1aSTA overexpression decreases trabecular CMs (Figure 3b).

claim: Cardiomyocyte-specific gain-of-function manipulations of glycolysis increase trabeculation.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of glycolysis impairs cardiac trabeculation, and cardiomyocyte-specific loss- and gain-of-function manipulations of glycolysis decrease and increase trabeculation, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that pdk3b overexpression increases trabecular CMs (Figure 3b).

claim: Loss of the glycolytic enzyme pyruvate kinase M2 impairs trabeculation.
source: In addition, loss of the glycolytic enzyme pyruvate kinase M2 impairs trabeculation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that pkma2; pkmb double mutants exhibit impaired trabeculation (Figure 4).

claim: Delaminating cardiomyocytes exhibit morphological changes during trabeculation.
source: We found that delaminating CMs exhibit morphological changes as well as rearrangements of contact sites (Figure 1b–c" and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–d"; Figure 1—videos 1 and 2), while CMs remaining in the compact layer do not exhibit such changes (Figure 1d–e").
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D time-course imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Delaminating cardiomyocytes exhibit rearrangements of contact sites during trabeculation.
source: We found that delaminating CMs exhibit morphological changes as well as rearrangements of contact sites (Figure 1b–c" and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–d"; Figure 1—videos 1 and 2), while CMs remaining in the compact layer do not exhibit such changes (Figure 1d–e").
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D time-course imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: N-cadherin localizes to protruding membranes in delaminating cardiomyocytes.
source: We observed that N-cadherin localizes to protruding membranes in delaminating CMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f–g") and to the lateral membranes of compact layer CMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h–i"), in agreement with a previous report (Cherian et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data and is consistent with previous published work.

claim: N-cadherin localizes to the lateral membranes of compact layer cardiomyocytes.
source: We observed that N-cadherin localizes to protruding membranes in delaminating CMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f–g") and to the lateral membranes of compact layer CMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h–i"), in agreement with a previous report (Cherian et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data and is consistent with previous published work.

claim: Cardiomyocytes display partial sarcomere disassembly in their protrusions when entering the trabecular layer.
source: We found that CMs display partial sarcomere disassembly in their protrusions when entering the trabecular layer (Figure 1f–g").
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data using LIFEACT-GFP to visualize sarcomere structure.

claim: Upon CAERBB2 overexpression, several glycolytic enzymes were upregulated in cardiomyocytes.
source: We found that upon CAERBB2 overexpression (OE), several glycolytic enzymes were upregulated, while mitochondrial proteins and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)-related enzymes were downregulated (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein expression analysis in a transgenic mouse model.

claim: Upon CAERBB2 overexpression, mitochondrial proteins and oxidative phosphorylation-related enzymes were downregulated in cardiomyocytes.
source: We found that upon CAERBB2 overexpression (OE), several glycolytic enzymes were upregulated, while mitochondrial proteins and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)-related enzymes were downregulated (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein expression analysis in a transgenic mouse model.

claim: Erbb2 overexpression upregulates many glycolytic enzyme genes in rat neonatal cardiomyocytes.
source: We also tested the effects of Erbb2 OE, which like CAErbb2 OE, activates downstream signaling (Pedersen et al., 2009), on the expression of glycolytic enzyme genes in rat neonatal CMs, and found that many of them were upregulated (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data and is consistent with known signaling effects.

claim: Erbb2 overexpression greatly upregulates the levels of pyruvate kinase M2 in rat neonatal cardiomyocytes.
source: Notably, we found that Erbb2 OE in rat neonatal CMs greatly upregulated the levels of pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2), a key glycolytic enzyme, (Figure 2b and c), and increased glycolytic activity as evidenced by measuring extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: Erbb2 overexpression increases glycolytic activity in rat neonatal cardiomyocytes as evidenced by measuring extracellular acidification rate.
source: Notably, we found that Erbb2 OE in rat neonatal CMs greatly upregulated the levels of pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2), a key glycolytic enzyme, (Figure 2b and c), and increased glycolytic activity as evidenced by measuring extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by ECAR measurements shown in Figure 2d.

claim: NRG1 stimulation activates glycolysis in rat neonatal cardiomyocytes.
source: NRG1 stimulation also activated glycolysis in rat neonatal CMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by ECAR measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Erbb2 inhibitor treatment severely affects trabeculation in zebrafish.
source: Moreover, we treated zebrafish embryos with an Erbb2 inhibitor (Figure 2e), which has been shown to severely affect trabeculation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) (Liu et al., 2010; Peshkovsky et al., 2011), and found that the cardiac expression of glycolytic enzyme genes was downregulated (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data and previous publications.

claim: Erbb2 inhibitor treatment downregulates the cardiac expression of glycolytic enzyme genes in zebrafish.
source: Moreover, we treated zebrafish embryos with an Erbb2 inhibitor (Figure 2e), which has been shown to severely affect trabeculation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) (Liu et al., 2010; Peshkovsky et al., 2011), and found that the cardiac expression of glycolytic enzyme genes was downregulated (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-coenzyme A.
source: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA), which enters the tricarboxylic acid cycle (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases inhibit PDC activity and enhance glycolysis in cardiomyocytes.
source: Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases (PDKs) inhibit PDC activity and enhance glycolysis in CMs (Zhao et al., 2008) and cancer cells (Koukourakis et al., 2005; Lu et al., 2008; Leclerc et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2018), thereby regulating the switch between glycolysis and OXPHOS (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: ERBB2 signaling positively regulates Pdk3 gene expression.
source: Our analyses show that ERBB2 signaling positively regulates Pdk3 gene as well as protein expression (Figure 2a and b and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and protein expression data.

claim: ERBB2 signaling positively regulates Pdk3 protein expression.
source: Our analyses show that ERBB2 signaling positively regulates Pdk3 gene as well as protein expression (Figure 2a and b and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and protein expression data.

claim: The PDK inhibitor dichloroacetate leads to a significant reduction in the number of cardiomyocytes in the trabecular layer.
source: Consistent with this model, we found that the PDK inhibitor dichloroacetate (DCA) led to a significant reduction in the number of CMs in the trabecular layer (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The phenotype caused by DCA treatment is similar to the one caused by Erbb2 inhibition.
source: Of note, this phenotype is similar to the one caused by Erbb2 inhibition (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative imaging data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Larvae expressing activated Pdha1a exhibit a significant decrease in the number of cardiomyocytes in the trabecular layer.
source: Notably, larvae expressing this activated form of Pdha1a exhibited a significant decrease in the number of CMs in the trabecular layer (Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Transgenic larvae overexpressing pdk3b exhibit a significant increase in the number of cardiomyocytes in the trabecular layer.
source: We also generated a Tg(myl7:pdk3b-P2A-tdTomato) line to overexpress pdk3b in CMs and thereby promotes glycolysis (Lu et al., 2008), and found that these transgenic larvae exhibited a significant increase in the number of CMs in the trabecular layer (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3b, and is consistent with the known function of pdk3b.

claim: Tg(myl7:pdha1aSTA-P2A-tdTomato) or Tg(myl7:pdk3b-P2A-tdTomato) larvae do not exhibit a significant change in the percentage of mVenus-gmnn+ cardiomyocytes compared to wild-type.
source: Next, we tested whether the modulation of glycolysis affected CM proliferation and found that Tg(myl7:pdha1aSTA-P2A-tdTomato) or Tg(myl7:pdk3b-P2A-tdTomato) larvae did not exhibit a significant change compared to WT in the percentage of mVenus-gmnn+ CMs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of proliferating CMs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Pdk3 overexpression leads to the induction of membrane protrusions in rat neonatal cardiomyocytes.
source: Furthermore, we examined whether the modulation of glycolysis affected CM morphology in rat neonatal CMs in culture and found that Pdk3 overexpression led to the induction of membrane protrusions (Figure 3d and d'), as well as cell-cell junction rearrangements (Figure 3d–d").
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Pdk3 overexpression leads to cell-cell junction rearrangements in rat neonatal cardiomyocytes.
source: Furthermore, we examined whether the modulation of glycolysis affected CM morphology in rat neonatal CMs in culture and found that Pdk3 overexpression led to the induction of membrane protrusions (Figure 3d and d'), as well as cell-cell junction rearrangements (Figure 3d–d").
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Erbb2 overexpression induces membrane protrusions in rat neonatal cardiomyocytes.
source: Similar effects were also observed following Erbb2 overexpression (Figure 3e–e").
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Erbb2 overexpression induces cell-cell junction rearrangements in rat neonatal cardiomyocytes.
source: Similar effects were also observed following Erbb2 overexpression (Figure 3e–e").
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Loss of PKM2 impairs glycolysis in endothelial cells.
source: Loss of PKM2 has been shown to impair glycolysis in endothelial cells (Stone et al., 2018), and PKM2 expression has been associated with glycolysis and cell growth in cancer cells (Christofk et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PKM2 expression is associated with glycolysis and cell growth in cancer cells.
source: Loss of PKM2 has been shown to impair glycolysis in endothelial cells (Stone et al., 2018), and PKM2 expression has been associated with glycolysis and cell growth in cancer cells (Christofk et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Zebrafish pkma2 is a splice variant of pkma and is an orthologue of mammalian Pkm2.
source: Zebrafish pkma2, a splice variant of pkma, and pkmb are the orthologues of mammalian Pkm2 (Stone et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Zebrafish pkmb is an orthologue of mammalian Pkm2.
source: Zebrafish pkma2, a splice variant of pkma, and pkmb are the orthologues of mammalian Pkm2 (Stone et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: During early development, pkma is expressed in the heart, head, spinal cord and blood vessels in zebrafish.
source: During early development, pkma is expressed in the heart, head, spinal cord and blood vessels, while pkmb is highly expressed in the somites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: During early development, pkmb is highly expressed in the somites in zebrafish.
source: During early development, pkma is expressed in the heart, head, spinal cord and blood vessels, while pkmb is highly expressed in the somites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: At later stages, pkmb becomes clearly expressed in the heart in zebrafish.
source: At later stages, pkmb becomes clearly expressed in the heart (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b; Gunawan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data and a citation to previous research.

claim: Loss of pkma2 and pkmb impairs trabeculation in zebrafish.
source: We examined pkma2; pkmb double mutants in which Pkma1, which drives pyruvate metabolism via OXPHOS, remains intact, and found that loss of pkma2 and pkmb impaired trabeculation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: There is no evidence for increased cardiomyocyte apoptosis in pkma2; pkmb double mutants compared to wild-type.
source: We did not find evidence for increased CM apoptosis in pkma2; pkmb double mutants compared to WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: There is a significantly lower percentage of pkma2; pkmb double mutant cardiomyocytes versus double heterozygous cardiomyocytes in the trabecular layer of mosaic hearts.
source: We found a significantly lower percentage of double mutant versus double heterozygous CMs in the trabecular layer of mosaic hearts (Figure 4b–c), indicating the importance of these genes in trabeculation.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell transplantation experiments and quantification shown in Figure 4b-c.

claim: Nrg1, Erbb2 and Erbb4 knockout mice fail to form trabeculae.
source: Nrg1, Erbb2 and Erbb4 knockout mice (Gassmann et al., 1995; Lee et al., 1995; Meyer and Birchmeier, 1995) and nrg2a (Rasouli and Stainier, 2017) and erbb2 (Liu et al., 2010) mutant fish fail to form trabeculae.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: nrg2a mutant zebrafish fail to form trabeculae.
source: Nrg1, Erbb2 and Erbb4 knockout mice (Gassmann et al., 1995; Lee et al., 1995; Meyer and Birchmeier, 1995) and nrg2a (Rasouli and Stainier, 2017) and erbb2 (Liu et al., 2010) mutant fish fail to form trabeculae.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: erbb2 mutant zebrafish fail to form trabeculae.
source: Nrg1, Erbb2 and Erbb4 knockout mice (Gassmann et al., 1995; Lee et al., 1995; Meyer and Birchmeier, 1995) and nrg2a (Rasouli and Stainier, 2017) and erbb2 (Liu et al., 2010) mutant fish fail to form trabeculae.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: NRGs are expressed by the endocardium.
source: NRGs are expressed by the endocardium (Corfas et al., 1995; Meyer and Birchmeier, 1995; Grego-Bessa et al., 2007; Rasouli and Stainier, 2017) and bind to ERBBs on CMs, triggering homo- or heterodimerization of ERBB family members and leading to activation of downstream pathways (Sanchez-Soria and Camenisch, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: NRGs bind to ERBBs on cardiomyocytes, triggering homo- or heterodimerization of ERBB family members.
source: NRGs are expressed by the endocardium (Corfas et al., 1995; Meyer and Birchmeier, 1995; Grego-Bessa et al., 2007; Rasouli and Stainier, 2017) and bind to ERBBs on CMs, triggering homo- or heterodimerization of ERBB family members and leading to activation of downstream pathways (Sanchez-Soria and Camenisch, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: NRG binding to ERBBs leads to activation of downstream pathways.
source: NRGs are expressed by the endocardium (Corfas et al., 1995; Meyer and Birchmeier, 1995; Grego-Bessa et al., 2007; Rasouli and Stainier, 2017) and bind to ERBBs on CMs, triggering homo- or heterodimerization of ERBB family members and leading to activation of downstream pathways (Sanchez-Soria and Camenisch, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Adult cardiomyocytes rely mostly on fatty acids as an energy substrate.
source: Adult CMs rely mostly on fatty acids as an energy substrate, and they are oxidized in mitochondria to generate ATP (Ellen Kreipke et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Fatty acids are oxidized in mitochondria to generate ATP in adult cardiomyocytes.
source: Adult CMs rely mostly on fatty acids as an energy substrate, and they are oxidized in mitochondria to generate ATP (Ellen Kreipke et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Under conditions of hypertrophic or ischemic stress, cardiomyocytes revert to glycolytic metabolism.
source: Under conditions of hypertrophic or ischemic stress, CMs revert to glycolytic metabolism (Doenst et al., 2013), which is characteristic of embryonic cardiomyocytes and uses glucose as a fuel.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Glycolytic metabolism is characteristic of embryonic cardiomyocytes.
source: Under conditions of hypertrophic or ischemic stress, CMs revert to glycolytic metabolism (Doenst et al., 2013), which is characteristic of embryonic cardiomyocytes and uses glucose as a fuel.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Glycolytic metabolism uses glucose as a fuel.
source: Under conditions of hypertrophic or ischemic stress, CMs revert to glycolytic metabolism (Doenst et al., 2013), which is characteristic of embryonic cardiomyocytes and uses glucose as a fuel.
evidence: The claim is based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Trabeculae facilitate efficient cardiac contraction prior to the formation of coronary vessels.
source: The outer wall of the developing ventricle consists of compact layer cardiomyocytes (CMs), while the inner wall consists of complex muscular ridges, termed trabeculae, which facilitate efficient cardiac contraction and oxygenation of the cardiac wall prior to the formation of coronary vessels (Sedmera et al., 2000; Staudt and Stainier, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Trabeculae facilitate oxygenation of the cardiac wall prior to the formation of coronary vessels.
source: The outer wall of the developing ventricle consists of compact layer cardiomyocytes (CMs), while the inner wall consists of complex muscular ridges, termed trabeculae, which facilitate efficient cardiac contraction and oxygenation of the cardiac wall prior to the formation of coronary vessels (Sedmera et al., 2000; Staudt and Stainier, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Disruption of ventricular wall morphogenesis is associated with congenital cardiac malformations.
source: Disruption of ventricular wall morphogenesis is associated with congenital cardiac malformations, the most common type of birth defects (Fahed et al., 2013), yet the cellular and molecular mechanisms regulating this complex process remain unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Congenital cardiac malformations are the most common type of birth defects.
source: Disruption of ventricular wall morphogenesis is associated with congenital cardiac malformations, the most common type of birth defects (Fahed et al., 2013), yet the cellular and molecular mechanisms regulating this complex process remain unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: During cardiac trabeculation in zebrafish and mouse, cardiomyocytes delaminate from the compact layer to seed the trabecular layer.
source: During cardiac trabeculation in zebrafish and mouse, CMs delaminate from the compact layer to seed the trabecular layer (Liu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2013; Staudt et al., 2014; Jiménez-Amilburu et al., 2016; Del Monte-Nieto et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cardiomyocyte behavior during trabeculation has been observed in zebrafish.
source: Although CM behavior during trabeculation has been observed in zebrafish (Staudt et al., 2014; Cherian et al., 2016), the 3D morphology of single cardiomyocytes during the trabeculation process needs to be further explored.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mammalian Pkm encodes two splice variants (M1 and M2 isoforms).
source: Mammalian Pkm encodes two splice variants (M1 and M2 isoforms); PKM2 plays an important role in glycolysis, while PKM1 promotes OXPHOS (Christofk et al., 2008; Lunt et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PKM2 plays an important role in glycolysis.
source: Mammalian Pkm encodes two splice variants (M1 and M2 isoforms); PKM2 plays an important role in glycolysis, while PKM1 promotes OXPHOS (Christofk et al., 2008; Lunt et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PKM1 promotes oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Mammalian Pkm encodes two splice variants (M1 and M2 isoforms); PKM2 plays an important role in glycolysis, while PKM1 promotes OXPHOS (Christofk et al., 2008; Lunt et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Before the onset of trabeculation, compact layer cardiomyocytes exhibit apicobasal polarity.
source: Before the onset of trabeculation, compact layer CMs exhibit apicobasal polarity, and then some of them depolarize and subsequently delaminate to seed the trabecular layer (Jiménez-Amilburu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Some compact layer cardiomyocytes depolarize and subsequently delaminate to seed the trabecular layer.
source: Before the onset of trabeculation, compact layer CMs exhibit apicobasal polarity, and then some of them depolarize and subsequently delaminate to seed the trabecular layer (Jiménez-Amilburu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: ERBB2 signaling induces EMT in breast cancer cells.
source: Notably, ERBB2 signaling, which is essential for trabeculation (Lee et al., 1995; Liu et al., 2010), induces EMT in breast cancer cells (Carpenter et al., 2015; Ingthorsson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Glycolysis enables rapid production of ATP to meet the high-energy demands of cell proliferation and migration in developing tissues, cancer cells and endothelial cells.
source: Glycolysis enables rapid production of ATP to meet the high-energy demands of cell proliferation and migration in developing tissues, cancer cells and endothelial cells (Lunt and Vander Heiden, 2011; Liberti and Locasale, 2016; Potente and Carmeliet, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Glycolytic intermediates are utilized to produce biomass including proteins and nucleic acids.
source: Moreover, glycolytic intermediates are utilized to produce biomass including proteins and nucleic acids, further supporting these processes (DeBerardinis et al., 2008; Potente and Carmeliet, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Excessive glycolysis is associated with EMT in cancer cells.
source: In addition, excessive glycolysis is associated with EMT in cancer cells (Peppicelli et al., 2014; Huang and Zong, 2017; Morandi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During trabeculation, cardiomyocytes exhibit membrane protrusions.
source: During trabeculation, CMs exhibit membrane protrusions (Staudt et al., 2014) and rearrange their cell-cell junctions (Cherian et al., 2016; Miao et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During trabeculation, cardiomyocytes rearrange their cell-cell junctions.
source: During trabeculation, CMs exhibit membrane protrusions (Staudt et al., 2014) and rearrange their cell-cell junctions (Cherian et al., 2016; Miao et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cardiomyocytes that enter the trabecular layer change their shape, similar to migrating cells.
source: Our 3D single CM imaging clearly reveals that CMs that enter the trabecular layer change their shape, similar to migrating cells, and lose cell-cell adhesion, indicating that they undergo phenotypic changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data and inference from the observed morphological changes.

claim: Cardiomyocytes that enter the trabecular layer lose cell-cell adhesion.
source: Our 3D single CM imaging clearly reveals that CMs that enter the trabecular layer change their shape, similar to migrating cells, and lose cell-cell adhesion, indicating that they undergo phenotypic changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing rearrangements of contact sites.

claim: Cardiomyocytes that enter the trabecular layer undergo phenotypic changes.
source: Our 3D single CM imaging clearly reveals that CMs that enter the trabecular layer change their shape, similar to migrating cells, and lose cell-cell adhesion, indicating that they undergo phenotypic changes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed morphological changes and loss of cell-cell adhesion.

claim: During trabeculation, cardiomyocytes undergo an EMT-like process triggered by ERBB2 signaling.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that during trabeculation CMs undergo an EMT-like process triggered by ERBB2 signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed phenotypic changes in CMs and the known role of ERBB2 signaling in inducing EMT in other cell types.

claim: Glycolysis regulates cardiomyocyte behavior during cardiac wall morphogenesis.
source: Our study reveals that glycolysis regulates CM behavior during cardiac wall morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental manipulations of glycolysis showing effects on trabeculation and CM morphology.

claim: Cardiomyocyte morphological changes regulated by glycolysis are important for delamination.
source: Together, these data suggest that CM morphological changes regulated by glycolysis are important for delamination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that glycolysis modulation affects both CM morphology and trabeculation.

claim: pkma2 and pkmb play important and cardiomyocyte-autonomous roles during trabeculation.
source: We found a significantly lower percentage of double mutant versus double heterozygous CMs in the trabecular layer of mosaic hearts (Figure 4b–c), indicating the importance of these genes in trabeculation.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell transplantation experiments showing cell-autonomous effects.

claim: Glycolysis plays important and cardiomyocyte-autonomous roles during trabeculation.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that glycolysis plays important and CM-autonomous roles during trabeculation.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including cell transplantation experiments and CM-specific transgenic manipulations.

claim: Activated Pdha1a contains mutations in its phosphorylation sites and is not inhibited by PDK.
source: This activated form of Pdha1a (Pdha1aSTA) contains mutations in its phosphorylation sites and thus is not inhibited by PDK.
evidence: The claim is based on the design of the mutant construct.

claim: Activated Pdha1a reduces glycolysis and enhances oxidative phosphorylation.
source: As a result, glycolysis is reduced and OXPHOS enhanced, as previously shown in cancer cells (Hitosugi et al., 2011; Fan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research in cancer cells.

claim: Erbb2 overexpression activates downstream signaling similar to CAErbb2 overexpression.
source: We also tested the effects of Erbb2 OE, which like CAErbb2 OE, activates downstream signaling (Pedersen et al., 2009), on the expression of glycolytic enzyme genes in rat neonatal CMs, and found that many of them were upregulated (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PDK3 is one of the key enzymes regulating glycolysis in delaminating cardiomyocytes in response to Erbb2 signaling.
source: Thus, we hypothesized that PDK3 was one of the key enzymes regulating glycolysis in delaminating CMs in response to Erbb2 signaling.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observation that ERBB2 signaling upregulates Pdk3 expression.

claim: Circularity of cardiomyocytes in the trabecular layer is significantly lower than in the compact layer.
source: (b) Circularity analysis of CMs in the compact and trabecular layers (n = 7–9 CMs from 3 to 5 ventricles).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: There is no significant deviation from wild-type in the number of trabecular cardiomyocytes in chimeric hearts with pkma2; pkmb mutant cells.
source: We also counted the number of trabecular CMs in these chimeric hearts and observed no significant deviation from WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.
